feedback: If you got 2.67, you divided 8 by 3 instead of 3 by 8. Re-read 3/8 as '3 shared among 8', which must be less than one whole — so it is 3 ÷ 8.
Model it concretely: 3 pizzas shared among 8 people gives each person less than half a pizza, so the answer must be below 1.
If you wrote 1/3 = 0.3, keep dividing 1 ÷ 3: the 3s never stop, so 1/3 is a little bigger than 0.3 and bigger than 30%.
If a division doesn't stop, that's expected for fractions like 1/3 — not every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal.
activities.intendedInsight: The fraction bar means 'divide the numerator by the denominator'; 3/8 is 3 ÷ 8, and some divisions (like 1 ÷ 3) produce recurring, non-terminating decimals.
learnerActions: Before dividing, predict: will 3/8 be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why (3 shared among 8 people is less than one whole).
Carry out the division 3.000 ÷ 8 step by step, keeping the decimal point and trailing zeros, to reach 0.375.
Compare the result against your prediction. If you predicted more than 1, check whether you divided 3 by 8 or 8 by 3.
Try a case that never stops: carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... keep repeating, and note it does NOT equal 0.3.
Round only when told to (e.g. 1/3 ≈ 0.333 to three decimal places), and explain why the division never terminates.
activities.title: Watch a fraction become a decimal: 3 ÷ 8

feedback: If you ranked 1/3 largest 'because 3 is a big number', convert first: 1/3 = 0.333..., which lands between 0.30 and 0.35.
Comparing by how big the written digits look is unreliable; the number line places each value by its converted size, so the order falls out of position.
To turn 30% into a comparable form, use that per cent means 'out of 100': 30% = 0.30 = 30/100.
If you treated 1/3 as exactly 0.3, place 1/3 and 0.3 as separate points — 1/3 is slightly to the right (0.333... > 0.30), so 1/3 > 30%.
activities.intendedInsight: Different forms cannot be reliably compared by surface digits; converting every item to one common form (then plotting on a line) makes the true order visible — and 1/3 sits between 30% and 0.35.
learnerActions: Take the set 30%, 1/3 and 0.35. First predict the order smallest→largest by eye, and say why.
Convert all three to ONE common form (decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35), using that percentages are hundredths and division for 1/3.
Plot each converted value on a 0-1 number line and read off the order from position, not appearance.
Compare your conversion-based order (30% < 1/3 < 0.35) with your by-eye prediction and note where they differed — especially whether you expected 1/3 to be biggest.
Transfer the method to a new set, e.g. 30%, 2/5, 0.35: convert each (0.30, 0.40, 0.35) and say where 2/5 goes, and why.
activities.title: Order a mixed set by converting to a common form

feedback: If you wrote 1/3 = 0.33 exactly, flag it as approximate: the decimal recurs (0.333...), so 1/3 is a touch above 0.33 and above 30%.
Use the hundredths/tenths link to move fluidly: 0.35 = 35% = 35/100 without any new division.
A triple-labelled bar is for consolidating recall; pair it with the division and ordering tasks to practise flexible conversion, not just memory.
activities.intendedInsight: Memorised landmark equivalents let you convert common cases instantly, reserving division for less familiar fractions, while a shared visual shows the three forms name one quantity.
learnerActions: For each landmark, show all three names on one shared bar or hundred-grid so the same shaded quantity is seen as fraction, decimal and percentage at once.

Match a form to its partners from memory (e.g. given 1/5, recall 0.2 and 20%); for fractions that are not landmarks, rewrite them as tenths or hundredths where easy (e.g. 3/20 = 15/100), and otherwise use division.
Note which landmarks are exact and which (like 1/3) are recurring, so you don't record 1/3 as a terminating 0.33.
activities.title: Build a landmark equivalence set
